q: How many IP addresses does Azure reserve in every subnet?
exp: Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet: the first (network address), the second (default gateway), the third and fourth (Azure DNS), and the last (broadcast). In 10.0.1.0/24, that's .0, .1, .2, .3 and .255. So any subnet has 5 fewer usable addresses than its size.

q: A subnet is 10.1.1.0/27. How many usable IP addresses does it have?
exp: A /27 contains 2^(32−27) = 32 addresses. Azure reserves 5 in every subnet (network, gateway, two DNS and broadcast), leaving 27 for VMs and other resources. 30 would be the usual non-Azure answer, which reserves only 2.

q: Two VNets both use 10.0.0.0/16 and must be peered. What's the problem?
opts: Peering requires non-overlapping address spaces, and these overlap completely
A /16 is too large to peer, so each VNet must first be reduced to a /24 range
exp: Peered VNets can't have overlapping address spaces, because routing couldn't tell which network an address belongs to. Two VNets that both use 10.0.0.0/16 overlap completely, so the peering is rejected. Re-address one of them, for example to 10.1.0.0/16. Region and VNet size aren't the problem.

q: VNet-A is peered with VNet-B, and VNet-B is peered with VNet-C. Can a VM in VNet-A reach a VM in VNet-C through these peerings alone?
opts: Yes, if they're in the same region
Only with a Basic load balancer
exp: VNet peering isn't transitive. A↔B and B↔C don't create A↔C. To connect A and C, either peer them directly or route through a network virtual appliance or gateway in B, with user-defined routes and 'Allow forwarded traffic'. Being in the same region doesn't change this.

q: Which peering settings let spoke VNets use a VPN gateway in the hub VNet?
opts: Hub: Allow gateway transit · Spoke: Use remote gateways
Both sides: Allow forwarded traffic only
Hub: Use remote gateways · Spoke: Allow gateway transit
exp: The hub owns the VPN gateway, so its side of each peering enables 'Allow gateway transit' to share it. Each spoke's side enables 'Use remote gateways' to use it, and then the spokes learn the on-premises routes. Reversing the settings doesn't work, and 'Allow forwarded traffic' alone doesn't share a gateway.

q: Global VNet peering connects:
opts: VNets in the same region only
Two subscriptions only if in the same tenant
exp: Global VNet peering connects VNets in different Azure regions over the Microsoft backbone. Regional peering connects VNets in the same region. On-premises connections use VPN or ExpressRoute, and peering works across subscriptions and tenants too.

q: Which statement describes a Standard SKU public IP?
opts: Dynamic allocation, open to all inbound traffic until an NSG is added
Static allocation, secure by default, with zone-redundancy support
exp: Standard SKU public IPs always use static allocation. They're secure by default — inbound traffic is blocked until an NSG allows it — and support zone-redundant or zonal deployment. Basic SKU public IPs, which could be dynamic and were open by default, were retired in September 2025. Public IPv4 addresses aren't free.

q: A subnet's effective route table has a system route, a BGP route, and a user-defined route for the same prefix. Which wins?
exp: Azure first picks the route with the longest (most specific) prefix. When several routes have the same prefix, a user-defined route wins over a BGP route, and BGP wins over a system route. That's how a UDR can force traffic through a firewall even when a gateway advertises the same range. Route age doesn't matter.

q: All outbound internet traffic from SubnetA must go through a firewall NVA at 10.0.100.4. Which UDR?
exp: A user-defined route with prefix 0.0.0.0/0 (all destinations) and next hop type Virtual appliance at 10.0.100.4, on SubnetA's route table, sends all outbound traffic to the firewall. Next hop Internet would bypass the firewall, None would drop everything, and a /32 route only covers the firewall's own address.

q: What does the next hop type 'None' do?
opts: Sends it to the VNet gateway
exp: The next hop type None drops all traffic to the route's prefix — a deliberate blackhole, for example to block a range. It doesn't fall back to default routing or send traffic anywhere.

q: A VM needs an IP that never changes, because a partner uses it in firewall rules. Configure:
opts: Any public IP; they never change
exp: A static public IP keeps the same address until you delete the IP resource, even if the VM is stopped or redeployed, so a partner can safely allow it in their firewall. Standard SKU public IPs are always static. A private IP isn't reachable from the internet, and a CNAME is a name rather than an IP.

q: VM1 can't reach VM2 in a peered VNet, and you suspect a routing problem. Which feature shows the routes actually applied to VM1's NIC?
exp: Effective routes (on the VM's network interface, or in Network Watcher) show the actual route table applied to the NIC: system routes, BGP routes from gateways and user-defined routes, and which one wins for each prefix. IP flow verify checks NSG rules, topology draws a diagram, and packet capture records traffic.

q: VMs in the same VNet must resolve each other by hostname using Azure-provided DNS. This works:
opts: Only with a custom DNS server
exp: Azure-provided DNS, at 168.63.129.16, automatically resolves the hostnames of VMs in the same VNet, with no setup. Across VNets you need a private DNS zone or your own DNS server, but within one VNet it just works.

q: Which TWO statements about VNet peering are true?
opts: Traffic between peered VNets stays on the Microsoft backbone, not the public internet
The peering status must be 'Connected' on both sides
Peered VNets share DNS settings automatically
Peering encrypts all traffic with IPsec
exp: Peered VNets talk over Microsoft's private backbone, never the public internet. A peering only works once both sides have been created and show Connected. Peering doesn't share DNS settings or encrypt traffic with IPsec (use a VPN, or encryption in the application, for that).

q: Which resources require their own dedicated subnet with a specific name?
exp: Some Azure services must be deployed into a dedicated subnet with an exact name: Azure Bastion needs AzureBastionSubnet, and VPN and ExpressRoute gateways need GatewaySubnet (Azure Firewall needs AzureFirewallSubnet). VMs can use any subnet, storage accounts don't live in subnets, and NSGs attach to subnets.

q: A VNet spans:
opts: A single region, including all its availability zones
One datacenter only, unless zones are added to it
exp: A VNet is a regional resource: it exists in one region and covers all the availability zones in it, so VMs in different zones can share one VNet. To connect regions, use global peering. A subscription can have many VNets.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: You can add address space to a VNet after creating it
A subnet can be associated with more than one route table
VNets in different subscriptions can be peered
The first VM in a subnet can take the x.x.x.1 address
exp: You can add address space to a VNet after it's created. A subnet can only be associated with one route table at a time. VNets in different subscriptions (even different tenants) can be peered. Azure reserves .0 to .3 in every subnet, so the first VM gets .4, not .1.

q: Order the steps so Spoke1 VMs can reach on-premises through the hub's VPN gateway:
items: Enable 'Use remote gateways' on the Spoke1 side
Verify that effective routes on a Spoke1 VM show on-prem prefixes
Enable 'Allow gateway transit' on the hub side
exp: First create the peering between the hub and Spoke1. Then enable 'Allow gateway transit' on the hub's side and 'Use remote gateways' on Spoke1's side (the hub must allow transit before the spoke can use it). Finally check effective routes on a Spoke1 VM to confirm the on-premises prefixes are learned through the gateway.

q: In what order are NSG rules processed?
exp: NSG rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first (100 before 200). As soon as a rule matches the traffic, processing stops and that rule's allow or deny applies. Alphabetical order and rule names don't matter.

q: A VM has NSGs on both its subnet and its NIC. What's the evaluation order for INBOUND traffic?
opts: NIC NSG first, then subnet NSG
Subnet NSG first, then NIC NSG
exp: For inbound traffic, Azure checks the subnet's NSG first and then the NIC's NSG; for outbound it's the NIC's NSG first and then the subnet's. Either way, traffic only gets through if both NSGs allow it. Priority numbers are only compared within one NSG.

q: Which default NSG rule lets VMs in a VNet talk to each other with no custom rules?
exp: Every NSG includes the default rule AllowVnetInBound (priority 65000), which allows traffic from anywhere in the virtual network (and peered or connected networks), so VMs can talk to each other with no custom rules. DenyAllInBound (65500) blocks everything else. There's no default rule allowing the internet or RDP.

q: An NSG has an inbound DENY for port 3389 at priority 200 and an ALLOW for 3389 from your office IP at priority 150. RDP from the office will:
opts: Be blocked; a deny rule always wins over any allow rule
Work; the priority 150 allow matches first and processing stops
Fail; office IPs can't be allowed
exp: NSG rules are checked from the lowest priority number. The allow at 150 matches RDP from the office first, so the traffic is allowed and the deny at 200 is never reached. A deny only wins if its number is lower. Reboots don't affect this.

q: What does it mean that NSGs are stateful?
opts: You must create a matching outbound rule for every inbound allow
Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically
Each rule applies once per day
exp: Stateful means an NSG tracks connections: if inbound traffic is allowed, its return traffic is automatically allowed outbound, and vice versa. You don't need a matching rule in the other direction. It doesn't mean rules survive deletion or apply once per day.

q: Application security groups let you:
opts: Encrypt traffic between groups of apps and use those groups as backend pools for load balancing
Group VM NICs by role and use those groups as the source or destination in NSG rules instead of IPs
exp: An application security group (ASG) is a label you put on VM network interfaces, for example asg-web or asg-db. NSG rules can then use the ASG as source or destination instead of IP addresses, so new VMs are covered just by joining the ASG. ASGs don't encrypt traffic, replace NSGs or scale apps.

q: What constraint applies when one NSG rule uses two ASGs (one as source, one as destination)?
opts: All NICs in both ASGs must be in the SAME virtual network
The ASGs must be in different regions
All NICs in both ASGs must use Premium SKU public IP addresses
exp: When an NSG rule uses ASGs as both source and destination, all the network interfaces in those ASGs must be in the same virtual network. ASGs used together like this can't span VNets. Different regions or a Premium SKU have nothing to do with it.

q: Which statement about service tags in NSG rules is true?
opts: They are Microsoft-managed groups of IP prefixes
Tags only work in Azure Firewall
You must update the IP ranges in a tag manually
exp: Service tags such as Storage, Sql, AzureLoadBalancer or Internet represent groups of IP prefixes that Microsoft keeps up to date. Using one in an NSG rule (for example 'allow outbound to Storage') means you never maintain IP lists yourself. They're current, work in NSGs and Azure Firewall, and update automatically.

q: Azure Bastion provides:
opts: Point-to-site VPN access to VNets over TLS 443, without a VPN client on the device
RDP/SSH to VMs through the portal over TLS 443, without public IPs on the VMs
exp: Azure Bastion is a managed service in your VNet that lets you RDP or SSH to VMs from the Azure portal over TLS (port 443). The VMs need no public IPs and no management ports open to the internet. It doesn't provide VPN access, a web application firewall or DNS.

q: What's required to deploy Azure Bastion in a VNet?
opts: A subnet named AzureBastionSubnet of at least /26, plus a Standard public IP for Bastion
Any subnet name, a /29 is fine
A subnet named GatewaySubnet of at least /29, plus public IPs on all the target VMs
exp: Azure Bastion needs a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, at least /26, and a Standard SKU public IP for the Bastion host. Target VMs don't need public IPs, and ExpressRoute isn't required. The Developer SKU is the exception: it's shared and doesn't need its own subnet.

q: Which capability requires the Bastion Standard SKU rather than Basic?
opts: RDP in the browser, session timeouts, and Entra ID sign-in to portal
Native client support, shareable links, and IP-based connections
exp: The Standard (and Premium) SKU of Bastion adds native client support (az network bastion rdp/ssh from your own RDP or SSH client), shareable links, connecting by IP address and scaling out. RDP and SSH in the browser to a VM already work on Basic.

q: What happens when you enable a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on a subnet?
opts: The storage account gets a private IP address in the subnet and loses its public endpoint
The storage firewall can allow that subnet, and traffic uses the Azure backbone
exp: A service endpoint sends traffic from the subnet to Azure Storage over the Microsoft backbone and identifies it as coming from that subnet, so the storage firewall can allow the subnet with a VNet rule. The storage account keeps its public endpoint and IP; nothing gets a private IP. Use a private endpoint for that.

q: What's the key difference between a private endpoint and a service endpoint?
opts: A private endpoint gives the PaaS resource a private IP in YOUR VNet
Private endpoints are free; service endpoints cost money
Service endpoints give the resource a private IP reachable from on-premises
exp: A private endpoint places a network interface with a private IP from your VNet in front of one PaaS resource, so traffic to it stays private. On-premises clients can reach it over VPN or ExpressRoute. A service endpoint only marks subnet traffic for the service's firewall, keeps the public IP, and doesn't work from on-premises. Private endpoints cost money, while service endpoints are free.

q: After you create a private endpoint for storage account contoso1 (blob), VNet clients must resolve contoso1.blob.core.windows.net to the private IP. Standard solution?
opts: A private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net linked to the VNet, with the endpoint's A record
A public DNS CNAME record for contoso1 that points to the private endpoint's NIC resource ID
Nothing; it's automatic in all cases
exp: After a private endpoint is created, contoso1.blob.core.windows.net is a CNAME to contoso1.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net. A private DNS zone named privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, linked to the VNet and holding the endpoint's A record, resolves that to the private IP. Editing every hosts file doesn't scale, and public DNS would return the public IP.

q: A VM can't receive traffic on port 8080 and several NSGs are involved. Fastest view of ALL rules applied to the VM's NIC?
exp: Effective security rules (on the VM's NIC, or in Network Watcher) combine the subnet NSG and the NIC NSG into the actual list of rules applied to that NIC, so you can see which rule affects port 8080. Advisor, the Activity log and Service Health don't show NSG evaluation.

q: What does Network Watcher IP flow verify tell you?
opts: The bandwidth and round-trip time of a link between two VMs, and which hop adds the most delay
Whether a specific 5-tuple flow to or from a VM is allowed or denied, and which NSG rule decided it
exp: IP flow verify tests one specific flow — source and destination IP, port and protocol — to or from a VM's NIC, and tells you whether NSGs allow or deny it and exactly which rule decided. It doesn't measure bandwidth, test DNS or calculate costs.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: One NSG can be associated with multiple subnets
NSGs can filter traffic using service tags and ASGs
Azure Bastion needs an NSG rule allowing RDP from the internet to the target VM
An NSG can be associated with a NIC and a subnet at the same time
exp: NSGs can be reused across subnets and support tags and ASGs; Bastion connects privately, so VMs only need RDP/SSH from the Bastion subnet; NIC and subnet NSGs can coexist.

q: You bought contoso.com from a registrar and want Azure DNS to host the zone. What do you configure at the registrar?
opts: A records for each Azure name server, pointing to the four public IPs of your zone
The domain's NS records, set to the four Azure DNS name servers of your zone
exp: To host contoso.com in Azure DNS, create the zone in Azure, then at your registrar replace the domain's name server (NS) records with the four Azure DNS name servers assigned to your zone. The internet then asks Azure for every record in the domain. A and MX records are created inside the zone, not at the registrar.

q: Which of these can an Azure DNS public zone NOT do?
opts: Host A, AAAA, CNAME, TXT, and MX records
Act as a domain registrar (buy domains)
Use alias records pointing to Azure public IPs
exp: Azure DNS hosts DNS zones: it can hold A, AAAA, CNAME, TXT, MX and other records, and alias records that point at Azure resources. It isn't a domain registrar, so you buy the domain elsewhere (for example App Service Domains or another registrar) and delegate it to Azure DNS.

q: What does auto-registration on a private DNS zone's VNet link do?
opts: Creates and updates A records automatically for VMs in the linked VNet
Issues and renews TLS certificates for VMs in the linked VNet
exp: When a VNet is linked to a private DNS zone with auto-registration enabled, Azure automatically creates an A record for each VM in that VNet and updates or removes it when the VM changes or is deleted. It doesn't register on-premises servers, issue certificates or block public DNS.

q: For one private DNS zone, how do the limits compare for registration-enabled VNet links and resolution-only links?
opts: Registration links are more limited (100) than resolution links (1,000)
Registration links are less limited (1,000) than resolution links (100)
exp: A private DNS zone can be linked to up to 1,000 VNets for name resolution, but only up to 100 of those links can have auto-registration enabled. Registration links are the scarcer kind. (Separately, each VNet can have auto-registration with only one private zone.)

q: Why is an alias record set useful in Azure DNS?
opts: It can point the zone apex at an Azure resource and follows IP changes
It replaces CNAME records everywhere, including at names outside Azure
exp: An alias record points a DNS name at an Azure resource, such as a public IP, Traffic Manager profile or Front Door, instead of a fixed value. It works at the zone apex (contoso.com), where CNAMEs aren't allowed, and updates automatically if the resource's IP changes. It works only for Azure resources inside Azure DNS.

q: Azure Load Balancer operates at which layer?
exp: Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4: it distributes TCP and UDP traffic by IP address and port, without looking at HTTP content. For Layer 7 features such as URL path routing, TLS termination or a web application firewall, use Application Gateway or Front Door.

q: Which load balancer SKU supports availability zones and has an SLA, and what applies to its public IP?
opts: Standard; its public IP must also be Standard SKU
Premium; its public IP can be either Basic or Standard
exp: The Standard Load Balancer supports availability zones, larger backend pools and HA ports, and has a 99.99% SLA. Its public frontend IP must also be Standard SKU — Basic and Standard resources can't be mixed. The Basic Load Balancer has been retired, and there's no Premium SKU.

q: A health probe fails for a backend VM. What does a Standard load balancer do?
opts: Stops sending NEW connections to that VM until the probe succeeds again
Restarts the VM and sends NEW connections once its agent reports as healthy
exp: When a backend VM fails its health probe, the load balancer stops sending new connections to it until the probe succeeds again. Existing connections aren't forcibly cut. The load balancer never deletes or restarts VMs, and doesn't send email (use Azure Monitor alerts for that).

q: Users must always reach the SAME backend VM for their session (a legacy app with local session state). Configure:
opts: Health probes with a longer interval
exp: By default the load balancer spreads traffic using a 5-tuple hash, so one user can land on different VMs. Setting session persistence to Client IP (or Client IP and protocol) always sends a client's IP to the same backend VM, which apps keeping local session state need. Floating IP and HA ports don't create affinity.

q: How does an internal Standard load balancer differ from a public one?
opts: It uses a private frontend IP from a VNet subnet
It can't have health probes or backend VM pools
exp: An internal Standard load balancer has a private frontend IP taken from a subnet, so only clients inside the VNet or connected networks (peering, VPN, ExpressRoute) can reach it. It's still Layer 4, supports health probes and uses the Standard SKU.

q: What is an HA ports rule (frontendPort=0, backendPort=0, protocol All) used for, and where is it available?
opts: Load balancing web apps on ports 80 and 443 only; PUBLIC Standard LB
Load balancing ALL ports and protocols; INTERNAL Standard LB only
exp: An HA ports rule (protocol All, ports 0) load-balances every TCP and UDP port with one rule. It's mainly used to put network virtual appliances (firewalls) behind a load balancer. It's available only on an internal Standard load balancer, not public or Basic ones.

q: You want to RDP to one specific VM behind a load balancer's single public IP (port 50001 → VM1:3389). Configure:
exp: An inbound NAT rule forwards one frontend port of the load balancer to a specific port on one backend VM — here 50001 to VM1:3389. Load-balancing rules spread traffic across the whole pool, outbound rules control outgoing SNAT, and UDRs route traffic between subnets.

q: HTTP requests must be routed by URL path (/images → pool1, /video → pool2), with TLS termination and a WAF. Why is Azure Load Balancer the wrong choice?
opts: Azure Load Balancer can't scale to more than one backend pool
Path routing, TLS termination, and WAF are Layer 7 features
exp: Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and can't see URLs, terminate TLS or inspect requests. Path-based routing, TLS termination and a web application firewall are Layer 7 features provided by Application Gateway with WAF. Load Balancer scales well and has health probes, so those aren't the reasons.

q: Backend VMs behind a new Standard public LB receive no traffic. The VMs are healthy and the rules look right. A classic cause is:
opts: No NSG rule allows the traffic
Port 445 is blocked by the ISP
exp: The Standard Load Balancer and Standard public IPs are secure by default: inbound traffic is blocked unless an NSG on the backend subnet or NICs allows it. Without an NSG rule allowing the port (for example TCP 80), healthy VMs never receive the traffic. Load balancers don't need restarting, and port 445 is unrelated.

ctx: The hub VNet (10.0.0.0/16) hosts a firewall NVA (10.0.1.4). Spokes VNet-App (10.1.0.0/16) and VNet-Db (10.2.0.0/16) are each peered to the hub only.
q: What lets App VMs reach Db VMs through the firewall?
opts: UDRs to 10.0.1.4 on the spokes, forwarded traffic allowed, and IP forwarding on the NVA
Nothing more — peering is transitive when both spokes are peered with the same hub VNet
exp: Peering isn't transitive, so the spokes can't reach each other through the hub on their own. Add user-defined routes on each spoke's subnets that send the other spoke's prefix to the firewall (10.0.1.4). Allow forwarded traffic on the peerings, and make sure IP forwarding is enabled on the firewall's NIC. Service endpoints and DNS don't route traffic.
